Thank you for resubmitting your work entitled "Fast and accurate edge orientation processing during object manipulation" for further consideration at eLife. Your revised article has been favorably reevaluated by Sabine Kastner (Senior Editor) and a Reviewing Editor.

The manuscript has been improved but there are some remaining issues that need to be addressed before acceptance, as outlined below: In the evaluation of the revision (which was sent back to the original reviewers), there was a consensus amongst all reviewers that, while the manuscript was substantially improved, some of the original concerns remained.

The open issues from items in the original summary are as follows:

1) The Model: All reviewers thought that the relocation of the model into the Results and expanded description have helped better integrate this with the main psychophysical findings. However, there remain two points of concern with this model.

The first concern centers on clarity of the revised description. The authors note that cutaneous mechanoreceptors in the human hand branch at their distal endings, and that SA1 and RA1 afferents are capable of spike generation at any and all of these branches. They propose that the receptive field sensitivity reflects the stimulation pattern of any and all of these branches. This is a very intriguing idea, but the model is not sufficiently described in the report. The basic idea is that subjects can distinguish whether particular afferents are included or excluded if the parent axon fires a spike. They illustrate a plausible mechanism for distinguishing 2 mm edges in Figure 5 in which arrows indicate the putative afferents that are included or excluded from the population response, and suggest that subjects might be able to distinguish the two orientations by recognizing which fibers are active, and which are silent. This is grossly oversimplified, because as two of the authors (Pruszynski and Johansson) have shown, individual afferents are able to summate responses from simultaneous stimulation of sensory branches, while others might not reach the spike threshold. The model also seems to assume all-or-none output from the individual sensory terminals. The model might be particularly useful for distinguishing the edge length effects, rather than the angular orientation of the edge. The best solution would be for the authors to present a formal description of their model, including equations used to distinguish orientations, rather than the simple graphics used in Figure 5. (Also, a minor note, the descriptor "toy model" is still used in the Figure legend; please correct this.).

Second, the hyperacuity model with connected subfields is proposed to explain the behavioral data. It is an intriguing model and it does outperform the traditional model with uniform receptive fields. However, this physiology-inspired model should be applicable for the active tasks as well as the traditional passive tasks (i.e., the model works regardless of active exploration along the skin). Thus it is still not clear how the model helps to resolve the discrepancy between the current findings (superior tactile acuity) and the previous finding (poor acuity). Moreover, the model does not relate to the hypothetical perception-action account that is favored by the authors. The authors need to better situate their model into the perception-action framework they use to argue the superiority of tactile acuity.

2) Active vs. Passive: The most important result of the paper is the impressive tactile acuity in the pointer-alignment task when compared with the poor performance reported in previous perceptual tasks. As was pointed out in the first review, this improvement is possibly a result of task difference, especially because the current task is an active touch task. In comparison, those passive perceptual estimation tasks typically put an edge stimulus perpendicularly against the skin (e.g., Peters, Staibano and Goldreich, 2015, which is also quoted by the authors). The large performance improvement by active touch has been known for nearly a century; for example, as pointed out by David Katz in 1925: "The full richness of the palpable world is opened up to the touch organ only through movements." Yet the authors basically discount this possibility in the Discussion: "However, provided that the skin deformations are similar to each other under active and passive conditions, active information seeking seems not to significantly improve spatial discrimination in perceptual tactile tasks (Lamb, 1983; Lederman, 1981; Vega-Bermudez, Johnson and Hsiao, 1991)." Interesting, the studies cited do not use the same passive conditions mentioned in the sentence. These "passive" conditions move the stimulus against an immobilized finger, as opposed to simply push an edge stimulus against the skin. Thus, when the authors wanted to show the superior performance they compared their active task against one type of "passive" task; when they tried to show that active information seeking does not improve edge discrimination, they quoted another type of "passive" task.

It seems clear that active touch is the main reason behind the superior tactile acuity reported here. The authors argue that "since the edges deformed the skin essentially through perpendicular skin indentation both in our task and in the perceptual tasks, it is unclear whether active touch contributed to the higher edge orientation sensitivity in our study." However, the pointer-alignment task not only has a perpendicular skin indentation, it also creates (at least) some sort of shear force when the finger moves the edge. This is a type of important sensory feedback for tactile processing of edge orientation, which should not be neglected.

The authors favor an alternative theory that tactile information is spatially processed in different ways for active tasks than for perceptual estimation tasks: "A third factor, which in our view may be most important for superior edge orientation sensitivity in object manipulation compared to perceptual tasks, concerns differences in how tactile information is spatially processed to support the behaviour in the two situations. In object manipulation, tactile information about edge orientation is naturally mapped onto the orientation of an object in external space and hence in the same space as the task goal. Moreover, because the object is mechanically coupled to the hand, the spatial transformation required to complete the task (i.e., object rotation) can be directly mapped onto motor commands." However, it is not clear how tactile information about edge orientation is naturally mapped onto the orientation of an object in external space for object manipulation, but not for perceptual estimation nor why spatial transformation (what exactly it is?) can be directly mapped onto motor commands can support superior tactile performance. The authors imply that their account is similar to the two-visual streams theory. However, to make this link, they need to prove or assume that the bottom-up tactile feedback is the same for the active and passive tasks. Since their pointer-alignment task involves very different tactile feedback than those perceptual estimation tasks, it is too early to make this link.

Thus, as with the second concern outlined in the critique of the model, the authors need to much better lay out their case as to the plausible mechanisms by which active movements improve this fine tactile acuity.

3) Task Description: The description of the task protocols remains opaque or misleading. For example, the authors categorize their task as a two-alternative forced choice protocol (presumably meaning that the subjects can choose to rotate the edge clockwise or counterclockwise), but as noted in the expanded Materials and methods: "A raised edge, centered on the plate [rest position of the hand during the intertrial interval] and spanning its entire length, was pointing towards the target position (i.e., 0°). […] The function of this edge was to offer the participants a tactile reference for the finger's home position." This means that the protocol is really a match-to-sample task, in which the test edge on each trial is compared to a standard edge that is easily matched when testing with the "infinite" edge. This distinction is important because the authors refer to spatial "working memory" in the main text [see subsection “Action versus perception”, second paragraph where the term is raised four times], in terms of the orientation on the previous trial: ".… direct sensorimotor information (visual, proprioceptive, efference) about the target position was last available ~3 s before the touch, i.e., at the end of the previous trial." This reference to working memory of earlier trials again appears in the subsection “Tactile versus visual acuity”, and” Neural mechanisms”, first paragraph. The subjects are presumably using the information learned during the intertrial interval when their finger rests on an "infinite edge" of the appropriate orientation.

At a minimum the authors need to specify in the main description of the task, in the first paragraph of the Results, that they have used a match-to-sample task, in which the sample is presented during the home position in the intertrial interval, and the subject needs to match the orientation of the test edge to that of the sample edge. Referring to memory of test edges on previous trials is inappropriate and indeed incorrect. Linking the test edge to that of the visual pointer used for feedback distorts what actually is needed for performance, although it may aid the subject in visualizing what is meant by orientation. All readers should be aware of the fact that the tactile cues were provided during the intertrial interval in the Results and Discussion, rather than being buried in the Materials and methods, as this is a critical feature of the task design that gets overlooked when interpreting the results.

claims.source: Taken together, we found that tactile information about edge orientation could effectively guide manipulation for edges that were 2 mm and longer and, with an edge of infinite length relative to the fingertip, alignment accuracy was, on average, better than 3°.
claims.evidence: This claim summarizes experimental findings from the main experiment.

claims.claim: The time between initial contact with the dial and the onset of the rotation was 0.20 ± 0.02 s.
claims.source: Averaged across participants' medians, the time between touch and rotation onset was 0.20 ± 0.02 s (Figure 3a).
claims.evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 3a.

claims.claim: Rotation onset typically occurred while the contact force was still increasing towards its plateau-like state.
claims.source: Rotation onset typically occurred while the contact force was still increasing towards its plateau-like state (Figures 1b and 3b), which, on average, was reached 0.31 ± 0.09 s after initial contact with the dial.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1b and 3b.

claims.claim: The contact force at rotation onset (1.15 ± 0.44 N) was typically smaller than the plateau force (1.64 ± 0.83 N).
claims.source: Accordingly, the contact force at rotation onset (1.15 ± 0.44 N, Figure 3c) was typically smaller than the plateau force (1.64 ± 0.83 N, Figure 3d; F1,9 = 11.5; p=0.008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements and statistical analysis.

claims.claim: Edge length and initial dial orientation showed no statistically significant effect on rotation onset time, time to plateau force, contact force at rotation onset, or plateau contact force.
claims.source: Edge length and initial dial orientation showed no statistically significant effect on any of these measures.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of experimental data.

claims.claim: The duration of dial rotation tended to increase with the required rotation amplitude.
claims.source: The duration of dial rotation tended to increase with the required rotation amplitude but the size of this effect depended on the edge length.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on analysis of experimental data on rotation duration.

claims.claim: Shorter edges that yielded smaller pointer displacements also yielded shorter rotation durations.
claims.source: Shorter edges that yielded smaller pointer displacements also yielded shorter rotation durations (Figure 3e).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3e.

claims.claim: None of the participants showed a significant relationship between the absolute alignment error and the rotation onset time.
claims.source: None of the participants showed a significant relationship between the absolute alignment error and the rotation onset time (0.01 < F1,399<3.86; 0.05 < P < 0.93, uncorrected for multiple comparisons).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis (ANCOVA) of experimental data.

claims.claim: None of the participants showed a significant relationship between rotation duration and absolute alignment error.
claims.source: In a corresponding analysis, we found that none of the participants showed a significant relationship between rotation duration and absolute alignment error (0.07 < F1,399<3.41; 0.07 < Puncorrected < 0.79).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of experimental data.

claims.claim: There was no reliable effect of the whole trial duration on absolute alignment error.
claims.source: Likewise, we found no reliable effect of the whole trial duration (that is, the entire time from touch to the end of the rotation) on absolute alignment error (0.01 < F1,399<6.17; 0.01 < Puncorrected < 0.92).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of experimental data.

claims.claim: Sub-movements were found in 44% of all trials.
claims.source: We found sub-movements in 44% of all trials.
claims.evidence: This claim is directly supported by analysis of experimental data.

claims.claim: The frequency distribution of trials with and without sub-movements was similar for all edge lengths.
claims.source: The frequency distribution of trials with and without sub-movements was similar for all edge lengths (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c) and trials with sub-movements were present in all participants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1d).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1c.

claims.claim: There was no significant effect of sub-movements on the absolute alignment error or on the proportion of rotations in the correct direction.
claims.source: Repeated measures ANOVAs with edge length, initial dial orientation, and presence of sub-movements as factors failed, however, to indicate a significant effect of sub-movements on the absolute alignment error (Figure 3—figure supplement 1e) or on the proportion of rotations in the correct direction (Figure 3—figure supplement 1f).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of experimental data.

claims.claim: Study participants generated the dial rotation action based on tactile information extracted and processed essentially within ~200 ms of initial contact.
claims.source: Taken together, these results suggest that study participants generated the dial rotation action based on tactile information extracted and processed essentially within ~200 ms of initial contact.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference based on multiple experimental findings about rotation onset time and lack of relationship between timing and accuracy.

claims.claim: Alignment performance was marginally better in the visual than in the tactile condition.
claims.source: Alignment performance was marginally better in the visual than in the tactile condition (Figure 4a,b).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of experimental data from visual and tactile conditions.

claims.claim: The absolute alignment in the visual condition (2.1 ± 0.5°) was smaller than in the tactile condition (2.9 ± 0.5°).
claims.source: The smaller absolute alignment in the visual condition (2.1 ± 0.5°) than in the tactile condition (2.9 ± 0.5°; F1,9 = 12.9, p=0.006) mainly stemmed from smaller errors in the visual trials with initial dial orientations closest to the 0˚ target (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements and statistical analysis.

claims.claim: The rotation onset time in the visual condition (0.07 ± 0.04 s) was shorter than in the tactile condition (0.20 ± 0.02 s).
claims.source: The rotation onset time in the visual condition (0.07 ± 0.04 s) was shorter than in the in tactile condition (0.20 ± 0.02 s; F1,9 = 201.5, p<10−6) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b), presumably because participants could program the movement based on visual information obtained before touching the dial.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements and statistical analysis.

claims.claim: The time from touch until contact force reached its plateau was modestly shorter in the visual condition (0.25 ± 0.10 s) compared to the tactile condition (0.31 ± 0.10 s).
claims.source: The time from touch until contact force reached its plateau was modestly shorter in the visual condition (0.25 ± 0.10 s as compared to 0.31 ± 0.10 s; F1,9 = 16.8, p=0.003; Figure 4—figure supplement 1c).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements and statistical analysis.

claims.claim: For all participants in the visual condition, the onset of the rotation occurred during contact force increase.
claims.source: Nevertheless, for all participants in the visual condition the onset of the rotation occurred during contact force increase.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on analysis of experimental data from the visual condition.

claims.claim: The sensory condition did not significantly influence the contact force at rotation onset or the plateau force.
claims.source: In fact, the sensory condition did not significantly influence the contact force at rotation onset or the plateau force (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d,e), and there were no statistically significant effects related to initial dial orientation on these timing and contact force parameters.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of experimental data comparing visual and tactile conditions.

claims.claim: The kinematic structure of the rotation movement was remarkably similar in the visual and tactile pointer-alignment trials.
claims.source: The kinematic structure of the rotation movement was remarkably similar in the visual and tactile pointer-alignment trials.
claims.evidence: This claim summarizes multiple comparisons of kinematic measures between visual and tactile conditions.

claims.claim: There was no statistically significant effect of sensory condition on rotation duration.
claims.source: First, we found no statistically significant effect of sensory condition on rotation duration (Figure 4—figure supplement 1f).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of experimental data.

claims.claim: In the visual condition, none of the participants showed a significant effect of rotation onset time or duration of pointer rotation on alignment error.
claims.source: Second, as for the tactile condition, in the visual condition none of the participants showed a significant effect of rotation onset time (0.011 < F1,100<3.72; 0.06 < Puncorrected < 0.92) or on the duration of the pointer rotation (0.002 < F1,100<2.47; 0.12 < Puncorrected < 0.96) on alignment error.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of experimental data from the visual condition.

claims.claim: The frequency distribution of sub-movements did not significantly differ between the visual and tactile conditions.
claims.source: Third, the frequency distribution of sub-movements did not significantly differ between the visual and tactile conditions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1g,h).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of experimental data.

claims.claim: The comparison of the tactile and the visual pointer-alignment trials revealed similar dial orientation accuracy and kinematics.
claims.source: Taken together, the comparison of the tactile and the visual pointer-alignment trials revealed similar dial orientation accuracy and kinematics.
claims.evidence: This claim summarizes multiple comparisons between visual and tactile conditions.

claims.claim: The prevailing model supporting tactile acuity suggests that spatial details of touched objects are resolved based on the relative discharge rates of first-order tactile neurons having partly overlapping receptive fields and Gaussian-like sensitivity profiles.
claims.source: The prevailing model supporting tactile acuity at the level we report above suggests that the spatial details of touched objects are resolved based on the relative discharge rates of first-order tactile neurons having partly overlapping receptive fields and Gaussian-like sensitivity profiles (Friedman et al., 2002; Dodson et al., 1998; Wheat et al., 1995; Saal et al., 2017; Loomis and Collins, 1978; Khalsa et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: This claim describes the prevailing model in the field, supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: First-order tactile neurons branch in the glabrous skin of the hand and innervate many spatially segregated mechanoreceptive transduction sites.
claims.source: Here, we propose an alternative explanation based on a generally overlooked feature of the peripheral apparatus – namely, that first order tactile neurons branch in the glabrous skin of the hand and innervate many spatially segregated mechanoreceptive transduction sites (Cauna, 1956; Cauna, 1959; Nolano et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claims.claim: This arrangement yields first-order tactile neurons with heterogeneous cutaneous receptive fields that include many highly sensitive zones or 'subfields', apparently randomly distributed within a circular or elliptical area typically covering five to ten papillary ridges.
claims.source: This arrangement yields first-order tactile neurons with heterogeneous cutaneous receptive fields that include many highly sensitive zones or 'subfields', apparently randomly distributed within a circular or elliptical area typically covering five to ten papillary ridges (Johansson, 1978; Phillips et al., 1992; Pruszynski and Johansson, 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous neurophysiological studies.

claims.claim: At the neuronal population level, the high degree of receptive field overlap in the fingertips implies that first-order tactile neuron subfields are highly intermingled.
claims.source: At the neuronal population level, the high degree of receptive field overlap in the fingertips implies that first-order tactile neuron subfields are highly intermingled (Figure 5a).
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference based on known receptive field properties, illustrated in Figure 5a.

claims.claim: For edge orientation processing, an edge contacting the skin at a certain location and orientation will primarily excite that subset of the neurons whose subfields spatially coincide with the edge.
claims.source: Thus, for edge orientation processing, an edge contacting the skin at a certain location and orientation will primarily excite that subset of the neurons whose subfields spatially coincide with the edge, while a different subset of neurons will be primarily excited for a slightly different edge orientation (Figure 5b).
claims.evidence: This claim is a theoretical proposal based on the subfield model, illustrated in Figure 5b.

claims.claim: A coincidence code could enable the requisite edge orientation acuity and would operate at a speed suitable for the control of manipulation.
claims.source: Such a coincidence code is attractive because it could enable the requisite edge orientation acuity and would operate at a speed suitable for the control of manipulation (Johansson and Birznieks, 2004).
claims.evidence: This claim is a theoretical proposal supported by citation to previous work on coincidence coding.

claims.claim: The model with subfields performed at levels slightly better than human participants, showing discrimination thresholds 1.3° for the infinite length edge to 13.1° for the 1 mm long edge.
claims.source: First, the model with subfields performed at levels slightly better than our human participants – showing discrimination thresholds 1.3° for the infinite length edge to 13.1° for the 1 mm long edge.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the results of the computational model presented in the study.

claims.claim: The model with subfields always outperformed the model with a uniform receptive field.
claims.source: Second, the model with subfields always outperformed the model with a uniform receptive field.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of two versions of the computational model.

claims.claim: The performance gap between the two models grew for shorter edges (infinite edge difference = 6.4°; 1 mm = 28.4°).
claims.source: Third, and perhaps most interestingly, the performance gap between the two models grew for shorter edges (infinite edge difference = 6.4°; 1 mm = 28.4°), suggesting that heterogeneous receptive fields are particularly beneficial for demanding tasks that utilize tactile information approaching the limits of the system's spatial resolution.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by results of the computational model and leads to an inference about the benefits of heterogeneous receptive fields.

claims.claim: Heterogeneous receptive fields are particularly beneficial for demanding tasks that utilize tactile information approaching the limits of the system's spatial resolution.
claims.source: Third, and perhaps most interestingly, the performance gap between the two models grew for shorter edges (infinite edge difference = 6.4°; 1 mm = 28.4°), suggesting that heterogeneous receptive fields are particularly beneficial for demanding tasks that utilize tactile information approaching the limits of the system's spatial resolution.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference based on the modeling results showing greater performance differences for shorter edges.

claims.claim: Tactile edge orientation acuity has previously been examined in perceptual discrimination and identification tasks.
claims.source: Tactile edge orientation acuity has previously been examined in perceptual discrimination and identification tasks.
claims.evidence: This claim refers to previous research in the field.

claims.claim: The threshold edge-length for 75% correct rotation direction was ~2 mm, which corresponds to the dimensions of the smallest of manageable objects in everyday tasks.
claims.source: Interestingly, the threshold edge-length for 75% correct rotation direction was ~2 mm (Figure 2d), which corresponds to the dimensions of the smallest of manageable objects in everyday tasks.
claims.evidence: This claim connects experimental findings to real-world manipulation tasks.

claims.claim: The dimensions of jewellery clasps or buttons designed to be as small as possible for aesthetic reasons rarely have edge lengths that go below ~2 mm.
claims.source: For example, the dimensions of jewellery clasps or buttons designed to be as small as possible for aesthetic reasons, rarely have edge lengths that go below ~2 mm.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on general knowledge about the design of small manipulable objects.

claims.claim: In all previous tasks examining edge orientation perception, the edge stimuli were externally applied to an immobilized finger.
claims.source: Whereas participants in our pointer-alignment task actively moved their finger to contact the object, in all previous tasks examining edge orientation perception, the edge stimuli were externally applied to an immobilized finger.
claims.evidence: This claim describes a methodological difference between the current study and previous perceptual studies.

claims.claim: Subtle differences in contact dynamics may contribute to increased acuity during active object manipulation.
claims.source: It is possible that subtle differences in contact dynamics contribute to increased acuity during active object manipulation.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential mechanisms underlying the observed differences.

claims.claim: Some additional information about orientation may be available during the rotation, which could be used to adjust ongoing motor commands generating the rotation.
claims.source: Moreover, although our results indicate that participants rapidly and accurately extract information about orientation prior to object rotation, some additional information about orientation may be available during the rotation, which could be used to adjust ongoing motor commands generating the rotation (see further below).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential online control mechanisms.

claims.claim: In perceptual tasks, participants reported orientation after the stimuli had been removed from the fingertip, requiring reports based on a memorized representation of the tactile stimuli, which decays over time.
claims.source: In the perceptual tasks previously used to assess tactile edge orientation sensitivity, participants reported orientation after the stimuli had been removed from the fingertip. Such reports must be based on a memorized representation of the tactile stimuli, which decays over time (Sinclair and Burton, 1996; Gallace and Spence, 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim describes a methodological feature of previous perceptual studies and its implications, supported by citations on memory decay.

claims.claim: Memory decay was reduced in the current task because the response was initiated very soon after the stimulus is contacted and while it remains in contact with the fingertip.
claims.source: Memory decay was reduced in our task because the response (i.e., dial rotation) was initiated very soon after the stimulus is contacted and while it remains in contact with the fingertip.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference about how the task design reduces memory demands.

claims.claim: The central processing of sensory information depends on task and context.
claims.source: Another factor that might contribute to differences in tactile edge orientation sensitivity in different situations is that the central processing of sensory information depends on task and context (Engel et al., 2001; Crapse and Sommer, 2008; Schroeder et al., 2010; Gazzaley and Nobre, 2012; Zagha et al., 2013; Manita et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on context-dependent sensory processing.

claims.claim: Visual information can be processed differently in motor and perceptual tasks.
claims.source: For example, it is well established that visual information can be processed differently in motor and perceptual tasks (Bridgeman, 2000; Kravitz et al., 2011; Milner and Goodale, 2006; Rossetti and Pisella, 2002; Weiskrantz, 1996) and that such difference partially reflect the engagement of different cortical processing pathways (Milner and Goodale, 2008; Ungerleider and Haxby, 1994).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on visual processing pathways.

claims.claim: The dorsal visual pathway, supporting action, is thought to compute real-time motor commands based on directly viewed object metrics.
claims.source: The dorsal visual pathway, supporting action, is thought to compute real-time motor commands based on directly viewed object metrics, and the ventral visual pathway, supporting perception, is thought to extract lasting and detailed information about objects via memory associations and recognition.
claims.evidence: This claim describes established knowledge about visual processing pathways.

claims.claim: The ventral visual pathway, supporting perception, is thought to extract lasting and detailed information about objects via memory associations and recognition.
claims.source: The dorsal visual pathway, supporting action, is thought to compute real-time motor commands based on directly viewed object metrics, and the ventral visual pathway, supporting perception, is thought to extract lasting and detailed information about objects via memory associations and recognition.
claims.evidence: This claim describes established knowledge about visual processing pathways.

claims.claim: Motor-related signals at different levels of the sensorimotor system can affect virtually all levels of the tactile processing pathway.
claims.source: For the somatosensory system, motor-related signals at different levels of the sensorimotor system can affect virtually all levels of the tactile processing pathway (Zagha et al., 2013; Manita et al., 2015; Canedo, 1997; Fanselow and Nicolelis, 1999; Lee et al., 2008; Seki and Fetz, 2012; Adams et al., 2013) and incoming tactile information can be predictively filtered during action, making it possible for the sensorimotor system to attenuate irrelevant inputs and highlight task-critical information (Chapman, 1994; Bays et al., 2005; Blakemore et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on sensorimotor interactions.

claims.claim: Incoming tactile information can be predictively filtered during action, making it possible for the sensorimotor system to attenuate irrelevant inputs and highlight task-critical information.
claims.source: For the somatosensory system, motor-related signals at different levels of the sensorimotor system can affect virtually all levels of the tactile processing pathway (Zagha et al., 2013; Manita et al., 2015; Canedo, 1997; Fanselow and Nicolelis, 1999; Lee et al., 2008; Seki and Fetz, 2012; Adams et al., 2013) and incoming tactile information can be predictively filtered during action, making it possible for the sensorimotor system to attenuate irrelevant inputs and highlight task-critical information (Chapman, 1994; Bays et al., 2005; Blakemore et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on predictive filtering in sensorimotor control.

claims.claim: Tool use is associated with dynamically remapping of space represented by central multisensory, predominantly tactile neurons.
claims.source: Since our task can be considered a tool-use task, it is also interesting to note that tool use is associated with dynamically remapping of space represented by central multisensory, predominantly tactile neurons (Maravita and Iriki, 2004; Brozzoli et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on tool use and spatial remapping.

claims.claim: The added time between touch and rotation onset in the tactile trials (~130 ms) represents the time actually required to extract and process tactile edge orientation information.
claims.source: Since the rotation movement could be programmed before touch in the visual trials, it seems reasonable to suggest that the added time between touch and rotation onset in the tactile trials (~130 ms) represents the time actually required to extract and process tactile edge orientation information.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference based on comparison of rotation onset times between visual and tactile conditions.

claims.claim: Fast acquisition and use of tactile information is in agreement with the automaticity by which tactile signals are used in other aspects of object manipulation.
claims.source: Such fast acquisition and use of tactile information is in agreement with the automaticity by which tactile signals are used in other aspects of object manipulation, including mechanisms supporting grasp stability (Johansson and Flanagan, 2009) and target-directed reaching guided by touch (Pruszynski et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim connects the current findings to previous research on tactile control of manipulation.

claims.claim: There was no effect of the fidelity of the sensory information (i.e. edge length) on the latency of the triggered action (i.e., the start of rotation).
claims.source: Likewise, as with other action patterns rapidly triggered by tactile events during unfolding manipulation (Pruszynski et al., 2016; Johansson and Westling, 1987), we found no effect of the fidelity of the sensory information (i.e. edge length) on the latency of the triggered action (i.e., the start of rotation).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing no effect of edge length on rotation onset time.

claims.claim: In perceptual studies, reaction time measures typically increase when the credibility of the sensory information decreases.
claims.source: This contrasts with typical results of perceptual studies where the reaction time measures typically increase when the credibility of the sensory information decreases (Pins and Bonnet, 1996).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous perceptual research.

claims.claim: The important tactile information used in the task was acquired very soon after the edge was initially touched and thus signalled by the dynamic responses in first order tactile neurons when the edge deformed the skin during the contact force increase.
claims.source: These results suggest that the important tactile information used in our task was acquired very soon after the edge was initially touched (Johansson and Birznieks, 2004) and thus signalled by the dynamic responses in first order tactile neurons when the edge deformed the skin during the contact force increase.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference based on experimental findings about timing and the lack of benefit from longer processing time.

claims.claim: Tactile afferent information available later during the rotation would have been restricted largely to gradually fading responses in some of the slowly adapting tactile neurons.
claims.source: Indeed, tactile afferent information available later during the rotation would have been restricted largely to gradually fading responses in some of the slowly adapting tactile neurons.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of tactile neuron response properties.

claims.claim: The dynamic response of first order tactile neurons seems highly informative for the perception of edge orientation since the duration of stimulation seems to marginally influence performance in psychophysical tests.
claims.source: Interestingly, the dynamic response of first order tactile neurons also seems highly informative for the perception of edge orientation since the duration of stimulation seems to marginally influence performance in psychophysical tests – indenting the fingertip with a 10 mm long bar for 400 ms compared to 100 ms only slightly improved average orientation identification threshold (from 26.6 to 23.4°) (Bensmaia et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous psychophysical study.

claims.claim: Both tasks primarily gauged the accuracy of movement planning before rotation onset, where touch specified the initial orientation of the dial in the tactile task and vision in the visual task.
claims.source: We justify our comparison by the fact that both tasks primarily gauged the accuracy of movement planning before rotation onset, where touch specified the initial orientation of the dial in the tactile task and vision in the visual task.
claims.evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the experimental design and what the tasks measure.

claims.claim: In both tasks, the information available for possible online control of the pointer's state during rotation was restricted to proprioceptive and/or efference information about the movement of the hand.
claims.source: Since there was no visual feedback during the rotational movement in any of the tasks, in both tasks the information available for possible online control of the pointer's state (position, velocity) was restricted to proprioceptive and/or efference information about the movement of the hand (Desmurget and Grafton, 2000).
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental design and supported by citation on motor control.

claims.claim: Tactile signals related to the orientation of the edge would provide information about the pointer's orientation relative to the fingertip rather than information about the pointer's orientation in external space.
claims.source: The fact that the edge was touched during the rotation in the tactile trial did not mean that tactile afferent signals from the fingertip conveyed information about the pointer's state during the rotation. Tactile signals related to the orientation of the edge would provide information about the pointer's orientation relative to the fingertip rather than information about the pointer's orientation in external space.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference about the reference frame of tactile information during rotation.

claims.claim: The dial offered negligible resistance to rotation due to its very low rotational friction and moment of inertia, limiting skin deformation changes related to rotation of the dial.
claims.source: Because of its very low rotational friction and moment of inertia (see Materials and methods), the dial offered negligible resistance to rotation, limiting skin deformation changes related to rotation of the dial (i.e., no rotational slips and virtually no twist forces impeding the movement occurred in the digit-dial interface during the rotation).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the physical properties of the apparatus described in the methods.

claims.claim: Signals mainly in slowly adaptive tactile neurons could have helped in the tactile task by facilitating possible proprioceptively based online control by gradually improving the assessment of the orientation of the edge relative to the fingertip during the ongoing movement.
claims.source: However, we cannot fully exclude that signals mainly in slowly adaptive tactile neurons could have helped in the tactile task by facilitating possible proprioceptively based online control by gradually improving the assessment of the orientation of the edge relative to the fingertip during the ongoing movement.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential contributions of slowly adapting neurons.

claims.claim: The actual sensitivity of the tactile apparatus to edge orientation must be better than indicated by the experiment.
claims.source: The actual sensitivity of the tactile apparatus to edge orientation must be better than indicated by our experiment, since our approach, though naturalistic, introduces several sources of information loss in this regard.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference about the true capabilities of the tactile system given experimental limitations.

claims.claim: Sources of information loss in the experiment include noise related to arm-hand coordination and postural actions, as well as information loss associated with memory decay.
claims.source: This would include noise related to arm-hand coordination and postural actions in our standing participants, as well as information loss associated with memory decay.
claims.evidence: This claim identifies specific sources of variability in the experimental task.

claims.claim: The edge orientation sensitivity revealed in the tactile pointer-alignment task substantially exceeds that predicted by the Shannon-Nyquist sampling theorem if assuming a pixel-like mosaic of tactile innervation determined by the density of relevant first-order tactile neurons in the human fingertips.
claims.source: Yet, the edge orientation sensitivity as revealed in our tactile pointer-alignment task substantially exceeds that predicted by the Shannon-Nyquist sampling theorem if assuming a pixel-like mosaic of tactile innervation determined by the density of relevant first-order tactile neurons in the human fingertips.
claims.evidence: This claim compares experimental results to theoretical predictions based on sampling theory.

claims.claim: With the 4 mm edge, the average alignment error (5.9°) corresponds to a position change of just 0.21 mm at the end of the edge if rotated around its center, which is very small in relation to the ~1 mm average spacing between receptive field centers in human fingertips.
claims.source: For example, with the 4 mm edge the average alignment error (5.9°) corresponds to a position change of just 0.21 mm at the end of the edge if rotated around its center, which is very small in relation to the ~1 mm average spacing between receptive field centers in human fingertips (Johansson and Vallbo, 1979) (Figure 2c).
claims.evidence: This claim combines experimental data with known anatomical facts to illustrate hyperacuity.

claims.claim: The ability of humans to perform spatial discrimination finer than that predicted by the average spacing between receptive field centers, termed hyperacuity, has been examined extensively in vision and has also been reported for touch.
claims.source: The ability of humans to perform spatial discrimination finer than that predicted by the average spacing between receptive field centers, termed hyperacuity, has been examined extensively in vision (Westheimer, 2012), but has also been reported for touch (Dodson et al., 1998; Wheat et al., 1995; Loomis, 1979).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on hyperacuity in vision and touch.

claims.claim: The currently accepted model supporting tactile hyperacuity centers on the assumption that first-order tactile neurons have simple Gaussian-like sensitivity profiles.
claims.source: The currently accepted model supporting tactile hyperacuity, built largely on neural recordings in monkeys, centers on the assumption that first-order tactile neurons have simple Gaussian-like sensitivity profiles; at the population level, this model proposes that spatial details are resolved by comparing the discharge rates of neurons – generally estimated over hundreds of milliseconds (Khalsa et al., 1998) – with neighbouring receptive fields via an unknown neural interpolation scheme (Friedman et al., 2002; Dodson et al., 1998; Wheat et al., 1995; Saal et al., 2017; Loomis and Collins, 1978).
claims.evidence: This claim describes the prevailing model in the field, supported by citations.

claims.claim: At the population level, the currently accepted model proposes that spatial details are resolved by comparing the discharge rates of neurons with neighbouring receptive fields via an unknown neural interpolation scheme.
claims.source: The currently accepted model supporting tactile hyperacuity, built largely on neural recordings in monkeys, centers on the assumption that first-order tactile neurons have simple Gaussian-like sensitivity profiles; at the population level, this model proposes that spatial details are resolved by comparing the discharge rates of neurons – generally estimated over hundreds of milliseconds (Khalsa et al., 1998) – with neighbouring receptive fields via an unknown neural interpolation scheme (Friedman et al., 2002; Dodson et al., 1998; Wheat et al., 1995; Saal et al., 2017; Loomis and Collins, 1978).
claims.evidence: This claim describes the prevailing model in the field, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The average spacing between subfields is substantially less than the average spacing between receptive field centers.
claims.source: Under our proposed scheme, the degree to which different edge orientations synchronously engage different subsets of neurons determines edge orientation resolution, which would be higher than predicted by the center-to-center spacing of the receptive fields because the average spacing between subfields is substantially less than the average spacing between receptive field centers.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference based on the proposed model of receptive field organization with subfields.

claims.claim: The massive divergence and convergence of first-order neurons in the periphery onto second and higher order neurons in the central nervous system, together with these neurons functioning as efficient coincidence detectors, could allow fast feedforward processing of spatially correlated spiking activity in ensembles of first-order neurons.
claims.source: That is, the massive divergence and convergence of first-order neurons in the periphery onto second and higher order neurons in the central nervous system (Jones, 2000), together with these neurons functioning as efficient coincidence detectors (König et al., 1996; Usrey, 2002), could allow fast feedforward processing of spatially correlated spiking activity in ensembles of first-order neurons (Pruszynski and Johansson, 2014; Johansson and Birznieks, 2004; Johansson and Flanagan, 2009; Jörntell et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is a theoretical proposal supported by citations to previous work on neural connectivity and coincidence detection.

claims.claim: The convergence of inputs from multiple mechanoreceptive transduction sites on individual first-order neurons (yielding subfields) represents an optimal scheme for preserving behaviourally relevant spatial tactile information given the relatively tight space constraints for neurons in the peripheral nerve and dorsal root ganglion as compared to mechanoreceptors in the skin.
claims.source: We believe that the convergence of inputs from multiple mechanoreceptive transduction sites on individual first-order neurons (yielding subfields) represents an optimal scheme for preserving behaviourally relevant spatial tactile information given the relatively tight space constraints for neurons in the peripheral nerve (axons) and dorsal root ganglion (cell bodies) as compared to mechanoreceptors in the skin (Zhao et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative claim about the evolutionary/functional rationale for the observed neural architecture.

claims.claim: Recent work from the field of compressed sensing shows that randomly sampling a sparse input signal often allows it to be fully reconstructed with fewer measurements than predicted by the Shannon-Nyquist theorem.
claims.source: For example, recent work from the field of compressed sensing shows that randomly sampling a sparse input signal often allows it to be fully reconstructed with fewer measurements than predicted by the Shannon-Nyquist theorem (Candes and Wakin, 2008; Candès et al., 2006), suggesting that heterogeneous connections in the tactile periphery may help overcome sensory processing bottlenecks related to pathway convergence (Candes and Wakin, 2008; Candès et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to work on compressed sensing.

results.result: Participants demonstrated exceptional tactile edge orientation acuity during object manipulation, achieving alignment accuracy better than 3° for infinite edges and 11° for 2 mm edges, substantially outperforming previous perceptual studies (10-20° for long edges, 90° for 2 mm edges) and matching visual performance.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C6, C10-C12, C17-C18, and C27 collectively provide strong experimental evidence for superior tactile acuity during manipulation. The data show statistically significant effects (C16), specific quantitative measurements with error bars (C17-C18), and direct comparisons to both prior perceptual work (C5) and visual performance (C11). The experimental design is sound with appropriate controls and sample sizes (N=10).

results.result: Tactile edge orientation information was extracted and processed remarkably quickly, with participants initiating appropriate dial rotation within ~200 ms of initial contact, and the added ~130 ms in tactile versus visual trials represents the time required for tactile processing.
results.evaluation: Claims C13, C28-C31, and C40 provide converging experimental evidence for rapid tactile processing. The 200 ms rotation onset time is directly measured (C28), occurs during force increase (C29-C30), and is independent of edge length (C31). The inference about ~130 ms processing time (C77) is reasonable based on comparison with visual trials, though this assumes no other differences between conditions.

results.result: Edge length systematically affected alignment performance: shorter edges increased errors through both increased wrong-direction rotations and poorer displacement scaling, with a threshold of ~2 mm for 75% correct direction discrimination.
results.evaluation: Claims C16, C19-C25 provide detailed statistical evidence (F-statistics, p-values) for systematic effects of edge length on multiple performance measures. The data show both main effects and interactions (C25), with appropriate statistical tests. The 2 mm threshold (C21) is derived using standard psychophysical criteria. The analysis appropriately separates direction errors from scaling errors.

results.result: Alignment accuracy was independent of rotation onset time, rotation duration, and trial duration, and the presence of sub-movements (44% of trials) did not improve performance, suggesting information was extracted rapidly at initial contact.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C39 provide statistical evidence from ANCOVA analyses showing no relationship between timing variables and accuracy across all participants. The sub-movement analysis (C37-C39) includes appropriate statistical tests (repeated measures ANOVA). These null results are important for understanding the temporal dynamics of tactile processing and support the interpretation in C40.

results.result: Tactile and visual pointer-alignment performance were remarkably similar in accuracy (2.9° vs 2.1°) and kinematics, with the main difference being faster rotation onset in visual trials (70 ms vs 200 ms) due to pre-programming.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C51 provide comprehensive comparison between tactile and visual conditions with appropriate statistical tests. The small but significant difference in accuracy (C42) is well-characterized, and the kinematic similarities (C47-C50) are documented across multiple measures. The interpretation of faster visual onset (C43) as reflecting pre-programming is reasonable given the experimental design.

results.result: A follow-up experiment with 50 initial orientations (instead of 6) confirmed that participants did not learn discrete responses but used analog tactile information, showing similar accuracy (2.7° vs 2.9°) to the main experiment.
results.evaluation: Claim C26 provides direct experimental evidence ruling out a discrete response strategy. The statistical comparison (F1,18=1.19, p=0.29) appropriately shows no significant difference. This control experiment strengthens the interpretation that participants genuinely processed edge orientation information rather than categorizing among learned responses.

results.result: A computational model with heterogeneous receptive fields containing subfields outperformed a uniform receptive field model and matched human performance, with the performance advantage growing for shorter edges (6.4° difference for infinite edges, 28.4° for 1 mm edges).
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C61 present modeling results that support the subfield hypothesis. The model performance (C58) matches experimental data, the comparison between models (C59-C60) is systematic, and the edge-length dependency (C60) provides specific predictions. However, the model makes simplifying assumptions and the discrimination criterion (5% change in population) is somewhat arbitrary.

results.result: The authors propose that first-order tactile neurons with branching anatomy and multiple subfields enable superior edge orientation processing through a coincidence code, where different edge orientations activate different subsets of neurons with intermingled subfields.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C15, C53-C57, C96-C97 present an anatomically-grounded theoretical proposal. The anatomical facts about branching (C14, C53) and subfields (C15, C54) are well-cited. However, the specific mechanism (C56-C57, C97) remains speculative. The proposal is plausible and consistent with the data, but direct neural evidence for this coding scheme during the task is lacking. The model (C58-C61) provides computational support but not physiological validation.

results.result: The superior tactile acuity in manipulation versus perception tasks may reflect multiple factors including active versus passive touch, reduced memory demands, task-dependent sensory processing, and differences between motor and perceptual pathways.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C8-C9, C62, C65-C76 discuss potential explanations for the discrepancy with prior perceptual studies. While the prior work is accurately cited (C8-C9) and multiple plausible mechanisms are discussed with appropriate citations (C70-C76), these remain speculative explanations (C66-C67). The manuscript appropriately acknowledges uncertainty about which factors are most important. Direct experimental tests of these mechanisms are not provided.

results.result: The lack of effect of edge length on rotation onset time, contrasting with typical perceptual studies, suggests that critical tactile information was acquired from dynamic neural responses during initial contact force increase rather than from sustained responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C83 provide a coherent interpretation of the timing data. The experimental finding (C79) is well-supported and contrasts appropriately with perceptual literature (C80). The inference about dynamic responses (C81) is reasonable given the timing and is supported by citation to prior work on neural responses (C83). However, direct neural recordings during the task would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: The tactile and visual tasks are comparable because both primarily assess movement planning accuracy, with limited online control available in either condition, though some contribution from slowly adapting neurons during rotation cannot be fully excluded.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C88 provide justification for the tactile-visual comparison. The reasoning about comparable information availability (C84-C85) is sound given the experimental design. The analysis of tactile information reference frames (C86) and apparatus properties (C87) is appropriate. The acknowledgment of uncertainty (C88) is scientifically appropriate, though this possibility seems unlikely given the null results in C34-C36.

results.result: The observed tactile acuity represents hyperacuity, exceeding predictions from Shannon-Nyquist sampling based on receptive field spacing (~1 mm), with the 4 mm edge showing 0.21 mm spatial resolution, challenging prevailing models based on Gaussian receptive fields and rate coding.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C95 appropriately contextualize the findings within the hyperacuity literature. The calculation (C92) correctly shows performance exceeding receptor spacing. The comparison to prevailing models (C94-C95) is well-cited. The inference that true sensitivity exceeds measured performance (C89-C90) is reasonable given identified noise sources. This provides strong motivation for the alternative model proposed.

results.result: The authors speculate that heterogeneous receptive fields with subfields may represent an optimal solution to spatial constraints in the peripheral nervous system, potentially leveraging compressed sensing principles to overcome convergence bottlenecks.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C100 present interesting theoretical speculation connecting tactile neural architecture to information theory and compressed sensing. While the compressed sensing literature is appropriately cited (C99), the application to tactile processing (C100) remains speculative. The evolutionary/functional argument (C98) is plausible but not directly tested. These ideas could motivate future work but lack empirical support in the current study.

results.result: Tactile edge orientation processing is critical for dexterous manipulation, and the ~2 mm threshold corresponds to the smallest manipulable objects in everyday tasks like jewelry clasps and buttons.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C7, C63-C64 provide appropriate context and ecological validity for the findings. The importance of tactile information for manipulation (C1, C7) is well-established and cited. The connection between the 2 mm threshold (C63) and real-world object dimensions (C64) is reasonable and provides functional interpretation, though the claim about minimum button/clasp dimensions (C64) is presented as general knowledge without specific citation.

results.result: Rotation duration increased with required rotation amplitude, with this effect modulated by edge length, such that shorter edges yielding smaller displacements also yielded shorter durations.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C33 describe kinematic relationships in the data with appropriate statistical support mentioned in the text (main effects and interaction). This is a straightforward descriptive finding about movement kinematics that is well-supported by the data shown in Figure 3e.

results.result: The fast tactile processing observed (~130 ms) is consistent with the automaticity of tactile signals in other manipulation contexts like grasp stability and touch-guided reaching.
results.evaluation: Claims C52 and C78 appropriately contextualize the speed findings within the broader manipulation literature. The comparison to other rapid tactile processes is well-cited (C78). This provides important context showing the current findings fit within established understanding of sensorimotor control, though it is primarily interpretive rather than presenting new data.
